notes.meaning: The Lord gave these dietary rules to Moses and Aaron together. Moses was the civil leader and lawgiver, while Aaron was the high priest who instructed the people in sacred duties. Both leaders were needed to teach the community how to tell the difference between clean and unclean things.

God began the food laws by telling Israel which land animals were permitted for food. An animal was clean only if it met two specific requirements: it had to chew the cud and have hooves completely split into two claws. These rules reminded the Israelites that they were God's special, chosen people, called to live differently from the nations around them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic commentary treats chewing the cud as a symbol of meditating on God's law, and the divided hoof as learning to divide good from evil.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest that clean animals were those that fit the normal order of creation, while creatures that seemed to blur boundaries between categories were considered abnormal and unclean.

notes.meaning: An animal was forbidden if it had only one of the two required signs. The camel chews the cud, but the underside of its foot has a soft, undivided pad rather than a fully split hoof. Because it lacked a completely divided hoof, God declared it unclean and unfit for Israel to eat.

The rock badger and the rabbit were also banned from the dinner table because their feet do not have divided hooves. While they appear to chew the cud because of their constantly moving jaws, they are not true cud-chewers in modern scientific terms. Moses used everyday observational language to describe what people saw rather than technical anatomy.

The pig has a fully split hoof, but it was strictly forbidden because it does not chew the cud. God commanded the Israelites not to eat pork or handle the dead bodies of any of these forbidden animals. Touching a dead carcass made an Israelite ceremonially unclean and reminded the people to avoid defilement.

God provided a simple guideline for identifying clean water creatures in both fresh and salt water. To be eaten, any swimming creature had to possess both fins and scales. Fish with these two features were viewed as healthy and wholesome food for God's covenant people.

Any water creature lacking either fins or scales was declared detestable. This rule ruled out shellfish like crabs and oysters, as well as creatures like eels and catfish. The command is repeated several times so Israel would strongly reject these foods and remain separated from pagan customs.

Instead of giving physical signs for clean birds, God gave a specific list of birds that were banned. These birds were birds of prey and scavengers, including eagles, vultures, and falcons. Eating birds that fed on blood and rotting meat was unacceptable for a holy people dedicated to the living God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that birds of prey were declared unclean primarily because they ingest blood and undrained meat from carrion, which the law strictly forbade Israelites to consume.

notes.meaning: The list of forbidden flying creatures continues with the raven family, the ostrich, and several kinds of hawks and owls. These creatures were known for eating carrion or living in barren wilderness wastelands. Since clean birds were not listed, ordinary birds like doves and pigeons were understood to be clean and allowed.

God also prohibited various types of owls along with water predators like the cormorant and the osprey. These birds are night hunters or diving fishers that feed on unclean animals and decaying material. God kept His people from creatures that lived in dark places or thrived on decay.

The list of forbidden winged creatures closes with water birds such as the stork and heron, as well as the hoopoe and the bat. Although the bat is a flying mammal rather than a bird, ancient people grouped all flying creatures together. Because the bat is active in the dark and does not fit the normal bird pattern, it was declared unclean.

Winged swarming creatures that crawl on the ground were detestable to the Israelites. The phrase 'walking on all fours' describes the creeping movement of insects close to the dirt, similar to four-footed beasts. Israel was not permitted to use common crawling bugs as everyday food.

God made an exception for winged insects that have long, jointed back legs designed for leaping off the ground. Insects belonging to the locust and grasshopper family were clean and could be eaten. In the ancient desert world, these hopping insects provided an abundant and nutritious source of food.

Every other kind of winged, crawling insect was strictly forbidden as food. Unless a flying insect had the distinct leaping legs described in the previous verse, it was considered detestable. God placed a clear line between the allowed jumping locusts and all other crawling insects.

Touching the dead body of any unclean creature made a person ceremonially defiled until evening. This was not a moral sin, but an outward condition of uncleanness that temporarily kept the person from the tabernacle. The sunset marked the start of a new day in Israel, ending the time of separation.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers view the rule of being unclean until evening primarily as a public health quarantine that prevented the spread of germs from decaying carcasses.
